units.title: 1. Cloud concepts and shared responsibility
units.description: Cloud service models, regions and zones, accounts and projects, shared responsibility, and cost basics.

lessons.title: Choose a cloud service model for a workload
lessons.summary: Choose a cloud service model for a workload. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: Cloud services offer computing resources through provider-managed infrastructure. Infrastructure as a service gives teams more control over virtual machines and networks; platform services manage more of the runtime; software as a service delivers a finished application. More managed services usually mean less infrastructure work and less low-level control.

The provider and customer share responsibilities, and the split depends on the service. A provider may maintain physical hosts while the customer still configures identities, data access, application security, and backups. Name the service and verify the responsibility model before assuming a task is covered.

quiz.question: In a managed database service, what responsibility usually remains with the customer?
options: Configure access, protect its data, and manage how the application uses it.
Nothing; the provider takes responsibility for the application and data.
Assume the system behavior without checking it.
quiz.explanation: Configure access, protect its data, and manage how the application uses it. Confirm it with relevant evidence and state any limits.

practice.title: Cloud concepts and shared responsibility
practice.prompt: A team wants less database patching work. What is the main tradeoff of managed service?
options: Choose the fastest action without checking impact.
Less routine infrastructure work, with some control delegated to the provider.
Unlimited access to the database host.
practice.explanation: Less routine infrastructure work, with some control delegated to the provider. This keeps the work scoped and reviewable.

lessons.title: Plan regions, availability, and cost
lessons.summary: Plan regions, availability, and cost. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: Regions are geographic areas; zones are separate locations within a region. Placing critical components across zones can reduce exposure to some local failures, but it does not automatically make a service resilient. Dependencies, data replication, health checks, and recovery procedures matter too.

Cloud billing follows resource usage and service choices. Estimate demand, identify an owner, set budgets and alerts, and remove resources that are no longer needed. Compare availability and cost requirements together; duplicate resources without a failure plan can add cost without delivering useful resilience.

units.title: 2. Compute, storage, and managed services
units.description: Virtual machines, object and block storage, managed databases, serverless basics, and workload selection.

lessons.title: Match compute to application behavior
lessons.summary: Match compute to application behavior. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: Virtual machines provide a general-purpose operating system; containers package an application and its runtime; serverless services abstract more infrastructure and often scale around events or requests. Each option changes how teams deploy, isolate, scale, and troubleshoot their software.

Choose the simplest operating model that meets the workload’s needs. A service needing custom host configuration may fit a VM; a portable web process may fit a container; a short event-driven task may fit a managed function. Consider runtime limits, scaling, portability, and who will operate it.

quiz.question: What is a sound way to plan for a single-zone outage?
options: Place required components across independent zones and test failover assumptions.
Use one zone and trust its name to guarantee uptime.
Assume the system behavior without checking it.
quiz.explanation: Place required components across independent zones and test failover assumptions. Confirm it with relevant evidence and state any limits.

lessons.title: Choose storage and protect its data
lessons.summary: Choose storage and protect its data. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: Object storage keeps durable objects addressed by keys and is useful for uploads, backups, and static assets. Block storage presents volumes to a machine; file storage provides shared filesystem access. Their access patterns, performance, sharing, and lifecycle options differ.

Classify data before choosing access and retention rules. Keep private data private, encrypt it appropriately, and define backup and deletion behavior. A backup is useful only if it can be restored; test recovery and record the time and gaps rather than relying only on a successful job status.

units.title: 3. Cloud networking
units.description: Virtual networks, subnets, routes, security groups, DNS, public and private connectivity, and segmentation.

lessons.title: Map virtual networks and traffic paths
lessons.summary: Map virtual networks and traffic paths. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: A virtual network defines an address space, subnets divide it, and route tables determine where traffic can travel. Security rules then constrain which connections are allowed. A common design places internet-facing entry points separately from private application and data components.

Names such as “private subnet” do not enforce privacy. Check effective routes, gateways, firewall rules, and service listeners. Allow only the paths a workload needs, then verify from both permitted and denied sources that the boundary behaves as intended.

quiz.question: What makes an application database private?
options: Its effective routes and access rules restrict connections to required sources.
The subnet is named “private.”
Assume the system behavior without checking it.
quiz.explanation: Its effective routes and access rules restrict connections to required sources. Confirm it with relevant evidence and state any limits.

practice.explanation: Allow the application path and deny unnecessary public reachability. This keeps the work scoped and reviewable.

lessons.title: Publish a service through DNS and a load balancer
lessons.summary: Publish a service through DNS and a load balancer. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: DNS records help clients locate a service by name. A load balancer routes traffic among backends, often using health checks, while a content delivery network can serve eligible content closer to users. TLS certificates protect connections to service names when configured correctly.

A request crosses multiple layers, and each can fail differently. DNS caching can delay updates; an unhealthy backend may still accept a TCP connection; a load balancer can have an incorrect health check. Trace the user’s path instead of treating all reachability problems as one network issue.

units.title: 4. Identity, data, and reliability
units.description: Identity and access, encryption concepts, secrets, backup strategies, availability, and recovery planning.

lessons.title: Grant scoped access to people and workloads
lessons.summary: Grant scoped access to people and workloads. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: Cloud identity systems grant permissions to users, groups, roles, and workloads. Least privilege scopes access to the actions and resources needed for a task. A workload identity avoids placing a long-lived credential directly in source code or a deployment script.

Separate duties, review permissions as roles change, and log sensitive operations. Prefer short-lived credentials and scoped policies. If a key is exposed, revoke or rotate it and examine audit records for use; removing a key from the visible code does not invalidate copies already made.

quiz.question: What is least privilege for a cloud workload?
options: A dedicated identity with only the actions and resources its task needs.
One permanent administrator key shared by the team.
Assume the system behavior without checking it.
quiz.explanation: A dedicated identity with only the actions and resources its task needs. Confirm it with relevant evidence and state any limits.

practice.title: Identity, data, and reliability

options: Choose the fastest action without checking impact.
Revoke or rotate it, then review logs and remove the exposure path.
Delete the visible line and assume the old credential is safe.
practice.explanation: Revoke or rotate it, then review logs and remove the exposure path. This keeps the work scoped and reviewable.

lessons.title: Protect data and test recovery
lessons.summary: Protect data and test recovery. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: Data protection includes classification, access control, encryption, secret handling, backup, and recovery. Encryption helps protect data at rest or in transit, but key access and application permissions still matter. Secrets such as API keys should be stored in managed secret systems and provided only to authorized workloads.

Recovery objectives should shape backup design. Decide what data must be restored and how quickly, then test a restore in a safe environment. Record what succeeded and what did not. A schedule or green job indicator alone cannot show that the application can recover.

units.title: 5. Deploy and operate a cloud workload
units.description: Deploy a small service, document architecture and cost assumptions, add logs and monitoring, and write a runbook.

lessons.title: Plan a safe deployment and rollback
lessons.summary: Plan a safe deployment and rollback. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: A deployment changes the version or configuration running in an environment. Rolling and canary approaches expose changes gradually; blue-green deployments keep a separate version ready to switch traffic. Each strategy needs health signals, ownership, and a decision rule for pausing or rollback.

Rollback plans must consider data migrations and external side effects as well as application code. Test the plan before production use. A deployment command returning success confirms only that the command completed; validate user-facing behavior and dependency health after the change.

quiz.question: A deployment passes build checks but increases user errors. What should happen?
options: Pause or roll back according to the release policy, then investigate the health signals.
Declare success because the deployment command completed.
Assume the system behavior without checking it.
quiz.explanation: Pause or roll back according to the release policy, then investigate the health signals. Confirm it with relevant evidence and state any limits.

Show only that a backup job started.
practice.explanation: Restore a sample and record what recovered and how long it took. This keeps the work scoped and reviewable.

lessons.title: Review service health, cost, and recovery
lessons.summary: Review service health, cost, and recovery. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: Operating a workload means observing its health, managing cost, responding to failures, and maintaining recovery options. Logs and metrics should answer operational questions without collecting secrets or unnecessary personal data. A runbook records first checks, contacts, and safe mitigation steps.

For a service review, show its components and data flows, who can deploy, where secrets live, how cost is estimated, and how recovery is tested. Use a non-production environment for practice and document limitations. Evidence makes the architecture more useful than a diagram alone.
